summary: Defines a URL scheme for referencing a POP mailbox, so a link can point to a mail account on a POP server.

eli5.summary: A web-style address that points to a mailbox instead of a web page.

questions: how to write a pop mailbox url
what is the default pop port in a url
how to write a pop url with apop
can a pop url contain a password
subtitle: A way to write the address of a POP mailbox as a link, with the server, port and login method in one string.

tldr.problem: Programs that read mail from a POP3 server need several settings (server, port, user, login method). Passing them around as one string is easier than passing each piece separately.
tldr.mechanism: The pop: URL scheme names the server and optionally a port, user name and authentication mechanism, in a form that puts the user and ;auth= mechanism before an at sign, then the host and port. Clear text passwords are not allowed in the URL.
tldr.outcome: A POP mailbox can be referred to like any other network resource. The RFC puts most of its care into warning clients not to send credentials to untrusted servers.

today: RFC 2384 is a Proposed Standard published in August 1998, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why a URL for a Mailbox
sections.content:
POP3 (RFC 1939) is described in this RFC as a widely deployed mail access protocol. To reach a mailbox a program needs several configuration elements, so a single string that carries them all is convenient.

A POP3 mailbox, like an IMAP4 mailbox, is a network resource, and URLs are a widely supported way to name network resources. The RFC points to ACAP (RFC 2244) as one case that needs such a string; there, an IMAP4 message store is usually written as an IMAP URL. This memo defines the equivalent POP URL scheme.
sections.eli5: Setting up a mail program means filling in lots of boxes. A POP URL packs all the answers into one short line, like writing your whole address on one envelope.

sections.title: The POP URL Syntax
sections.content:
A POP URL names a POP server and, optionally, a port number, an authentication mechanism, an authentication ID and an authorization ID. It follows the common Internet scheme syntax of RFC 1738, with one exception: clear text passwords are not permitted. If the port is left out, it defaults to 110.

The general form is pop://<user>;auth=<auth>@<host>:<port>. Everything except pop:// and the host may be omitted. The RFC gives the exact grammar in ABNF in its Section 8.
sections.eli5: The address has a fixed order: who you are, how you prove it, which computer, and which door on that computer. Only the computer's name is a must.

sections.title: User Name and Authentication Mechanism
sections.content:
The user name is used in a USER, APOP, AUTH (RFC 1734) or extension command after the client connects. If the URL gives no user name, the program SHOULD ask the user for one.

A mechanism is added to the end of the user name as ;AUTH=<enc-auth-type>. Without a leading + it names a SASL (RFC 2222) mechanism. With a leading + it is either APOP or an extension mechanism. When a mechanism is given, the client SHOULD use the matching AUTH, APOP or extension command instead of USER.

The string ;AUTH=* means the client SHOULD pick a suitable mechanism and MAY use any that the server supports. If a user name appears with no mechanism, ;AUTH=* is assumed. If a specific mechanism is named, the client SHOULD NOT switch to a different one without explicit user permission.
sections.eli5: The address can say how you will prove who you are, like a password trick or a secret handshake. A star means the mail program may choose any trick the server knows.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The RFC shows three URLs and the POP commands a client might turn them into.

  • pop://rg@mailsrv.qualcomm.com: the client asks the user for a password, connects to port 110, and sends USER rg then PASS secret.
  • pop://rg;AUTH=+APOP@mail.eudora.com:8110: the client asks for a password, connects to port 8110, and sends an APOP command with a digest instead of the password.
  • pop://baz;AUTH=SCRAM-MD5@foo.bar: the client connects to port 110 and runs an AUTH SCRAM-MD5 exchange of challenges and responses.
sections.eli5: Each address becomes a short conversation with the mail server: say who you are, prove it, and the server tells you how many messages wait for you.

sections.title: Encoding and Relative URLs
sections.content:
Relative POP URLs are not permitted, so a POP URL is always written in full.

Unsafe or reserved characters such as a space or ; in the user name or authentication mechanism MUST be encoded as described in RFC 1738. Because 8-bit characters are not permitted in URLs, UTF-8 characters (RFC 2279) are encoded the way the URL specification requires.
sections.eli5: Odd characters like spaces cannot go in an address as they are, so they get swapped for safe codes.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
URLs can easily come from untrusted sources, and sending credentials to the wrong server can compromise an account. Before resolving a URL that needs authentication, the program should check that at least one of these holds: the URL comes from a trusted source; local site policy permits connecting to that server; the user confirms the connection; the mechanism validates the server before credentials are sent; or the mechanism reveals nothing that could harm future connections.

A URL with ;AUTH=* deserves extra care because it might fall back to a weaker mechanism. Clients are discouraged from falling back to a plain text password unless the connection has strong encryption, with a key length greater than 56 bits given as an example.

Many email clients store the plain text password for later use. Such clients MUST NOT use a stored password in response to a POP URL without explicit permission from the user to give it to that host name.
sections.eli5: A link could trick your mail program into handing your password to a stranger. So the program has to be careful and ask you first.

data.title: POP URL ABNF
data.code:
pop-url          = "pop://" server
server           = [user-auth "@"] hostport
user-auth        = enc-user [auth]
auth             = ";AUTH=" ( "*" / enc-auth-type )
enc-auth-type    = enc-sasl / enc-ext
enc-ext          = "+" ("APOP" / 1*achar)
enc-sasl         = 1*achar
enc-user         = 1*achar
